7The ultracode pair

Opus and Fable each designed the workflow it would run with cost no constraint. Both cut the work into more than twenty units and check each unit several times. Priced on batch 10, they write 31M and 37M and take about 27 h and 36 h Pricing §2.

How they were briefed, and why

  • The first four weighed cost. Each was asked for an estimate and given prices: batch 9's costs for the first pair, the machine's prices for the blind pair. Your reading at 10:59 UTC: all four improve our process under a cost constraint, and that is not what you wanted to weigh Held.
  • What you asked for: Opus and Fable each design the workflow it would run in ultracode mode. The most exhaustive correct result, token cost no constraint, any granularity. Design only, no estimate asked Held.
  • What you are weighing: dropping the fixed workflow, and letting a Fable or Opus coordinator design an ultracode workflow for each batch Held.
  • Your condition: such a designer must not reinvent how to work safely and efficiently here: caches, builds, recovery after restarts, how long things take, when the full suite is needed, running one test Held.
  • So a project skill came first, fortress-repo: a main page and sixteen reference parts on builds and caches, worktrees, writing and running tests, the gate, the two measurements, the machine, recovery after a stop, committing, the toolchain, each area of the tree, and its sources Skill. It is not committed; it waits on your approval Held.
  • What they read: the blind brief's content and rules (the Opus designer also its machine file), the skill, the source, the specification, the ledger and repo-internals.md. No batch record, workflow script or other design Ultra Opus header Ultra Fable header.

The ultracode Opus design

Shape: three workflows in turn, plan, build and integrate; the coordinator reads each one's result before it starts the next. The work is cut into 22 units: W into 2, C into 8, G into 5 library sections, N into 7 Ultra Opus §1.

Before the launch the coordinator builds the base once; every worktree is a 3 s seed of it Ultra Opus §1.

Two mechanisms run through it. A run registry, keyed by the content of the code, records every build and run; no agent builds or runs without asking it first (rule 3). And every agent can be run again: it reads its worktree, branch, progress note and the registry, and continues at the first step not done Ultra Opus §1.

Tiers, its own choice Ultra Opus §1:

  • Fable "where a subtle wrong answer would pass every test": the walk and checker implementers of the hard tasks, the piece judges, the semantic refuters, the cross-piece reviewer and the final judge.
  • Opus for planners, critics, library implementers, mergers, readers and the report.
  • Sonnet for audits, form checks, and the agents that start and watch long runs.
  1. Plan85 agents; writes no file of the tree
    • Sonnet ×4 Audits check every claim of the brief against the base: files, lines, tests, rows, counts. A missing one stops the step.
    • Opus ×22 Planners, one per unit: the cause, the precedent, the tests, the fix, the specification text, the way not taken.
    • Opus ×54 Critics, two or three per plan, each with one lens: the standard, reach and tests for W and C; library practice and what a repair clears for G and N. Told to object when unsure.
    • Fable ×4 Piece judges settle every objection and write each piece's final plan.
    • Opus ×1 Cross-reader looks for interactions between the four plans.

    Priced: 12.1M, about 8.7 h Pricing §3.5

  2. Build121 agents
    • Fable ×5 Opus ×17 Implementers, test first: the test committed alone and seen failing through the harness before the fix. No whole suite.
    • Opus ×2 Piece merges join W's and C's tasks, one build each.
    • Sonnet Launchers start each piece's suites and measurements in the background, once per code state.
    • Lenses, 19 in the first round, none sharing the implementer's context: semantics on Fable for W and C, with probe programs run on the piece's build and the base's side by side; library practice, reach and the measurement site by site on Opus; the specification's form, guard tests and process on Sonnet.
    • Opus ×3 Refuters per serious finding. What two of them cannot refute goes to a fixer on the piece's implementer tier, test first. The touched lenses run again, until a round finds nothing or three rounds have passed.

    Priced: 16.6M, about 14.9 h, taking 13 serious findings over three rounds Pricing §3.5

  3. Integrate14 agents
    • Opus Merge-all merges the four pieces and writes the ledger, FACTS and PLAN lines in one records commit.
    • Sonnet ×5 The gate in five steps on the merged tree.
    • Fable Cross-review beside it: do the four pieces compose.
    • Opus Gate read against the last landed summary, and a reconciliation of the 340 base distance sites, site by site.
    • Fable, max effort Final judge asks for evidence for every "what done means" item and every rule, and says GO or NO-GO.
    • Opus Report, then Sonnet audits of the whole range. The coordinator lands on your go.

    Priced: 2.3M, about 2.6 h Pricing §3.5

Restarts. The step will cross the 13-hour process stop at least once. Each workflow's arguments are saved byte for byte, and a stopped workflow resumes from its journal; finished agents keep their results. An agent run again finds its pushed branch, progress note and registry rows, and continues. A background run outlives the process and shows in the registry, so nobody starts a second copy. The coordinator sets check-ins 45 minutes apart and one just after the predicted stop Ultra Opus §3.3.

What it puts to you Ultra Opus §4:

  • D1: rule 1 for library repairs that only the checker sees (below).
  • D2: whether the measurement record (gate summary, tables, per-site list) is part of "its report". It commits them with the report.
  • D3: the base. The brief describes an earlier commit than today's main; the run needs that commit's full hash.
  • D4: whether a GO lands at once or waits for your reading.
  • D5: Fable's pool. If it is short, the implementers move to Opus at the highest effort first; judges and refuters stay on Fable.
  • D6 and D7: branch names and the report folder; the common preamble as a project agent type, read from the cache, which must exist before the launch.
  • Eight measurements first, among them free disk, memory with a suite beside the distance, whether the tools keep their temporary files out of /tmp, and the time of the next process stop.

Priced on batch 10 as run: about 220 agents, 31.0M (22M to 45M), of it Fable 5.38M. About 27 h in three workflows (22 to 35 h), past the process stop at least twice Pricing §3.5. No estimate of its own; none was asked.

The ultracode Fable design

Shape: five workflows in turn: read, build, review, integrate and gate, record and land. The coordinator, a Fable session, reads the results between them. Each piece gets its own branch in a worktree seeded from one base build. The work is cut into 24 groups: a defect or a crash for W and C, a library section for G and N Ultra Fable §1.

Why this shape, in its words: with two slots on four cores, running the pieces two abreast is the only parallelism that pays, "so the fan-out goes into reading and review (which judge) rather than into implementation (which builds)" Ultra Fable §1.

Tiers, its own choice Ultra Fable §1, §2:

  • Fable at maximum effort for every reading, judgement, edit and repair, the merge and the records.
  • Sonnet for what the tree itself answers: the audits, the seeding, the gate run, the record check, the landing.
  • Opus once: the refuter who recomputes the measurement's site mapping, "a different tier for a different blind spot".
  1. Read97 agents; edits nothing
    • Fable ×48 Readers, two per group, from different starting points: one from the error outward, one from the specification passage and the library's precedents inward. Probes only on the base build.
    • Fable ×16 Adjudicators settle each pair against the code into a work order: the cause, the precedent, the edit as a sketch, the tests with their values, the sites to leave with a row.
    • Fable ×32 Panels for the eight hardest groups (rows 593, 604, 597, 588 and the four crashes): three independent approaches and a judge each, in place of the adjudicator.
    • Fable ×1 Boundary auditor reads all 24 work orders at once, for two pieces touching one declaration.

    Priced: 15.5M, about 15.1 h Pricing §3.6

  2. Build33 agents
    • Fable ×4 Tests first, one per piece: all the piece's tests, one test-only commit per group, seen failing on the unedited seeded worktree.
    • Fable ×24 Fixers, one fresh agent per group, in turn on the piece's branch.
    • Fable ×4 Finishers run the piece's suite once and the measurements once, map the per-site list through the diff, and write the piece report.
    • Heavy runs (a whole suite, the distance, the gate) are queued one at a time across the machine.

    Priced: 6.4M, about 7.3 h Pricing §3.6

  3. Review74 agents; up to three rounds a piece
    • Sonnet ×2 Audits per piece and round: the scope, and the order of test and fix commits.
    • Fable ×2 Opus ×1 Refuters: library practice and the cited passage; blast radius; the measurement recomputed.
    • Fable Completeness critic walks the brief's "What done means" item by item.
    • Fable Repair of a blocking finding. A repair that touches code sends the piece back through its finisher.

    Priced: 13.7M, about 10.5 h, taking two rounds for W and G and three for C and N Pricing §3.6

  4. Integrate, record, landabout 7 agents
    • Fable Merger. Sonnet gate on a clean build, after an 8 s walk run that loads the whole library under W's new checks. On red, a Fable triage and fix, at most three times. A Fable distance reader.
    • Fable Records agent, alone; a Sonnet verifier and lander. main moves by fast-forward only.

    Priced: 1.2M, about 2.4 h Pricing §3.6

Restarts. Five workflows, each resumed with the same script and arguments, byte for byte; no clock or random value in a script. Every agent starts by recovering from its worktree's git log, its progress file and its logs' exit lines, and continues. A live background run is waited for, not restarted. Every commit is pushed at once. An empty return is retried once; a second marks the group blocked and the step goes on. Check-ins every 45 minutes and one after the predicted stop; the coordinator never presses stop. After a new session it rebuilds the next workflow's arguments from the pushed branches and the journal Ultra Fable §3.

What it puts to you Ultra Fable §4:

  • 1: rule 1 for library sites no walk test can see fail (below). Its first question.
  • 2: a testSystem run on G's and N's final code, two 4-minute runs, so a regression is traced to its piece before the merge.
  • 3: the record's folder and form, and whether main keeps the four merges or a straight history.
  • 4: the base build holds one untracked file, BASE_COMMIT, which the seeding script refuses.
  • 5 and 6: the slot count, project agent types for the preamble, and timing one reader and one group fix before the run.
  • 7: a number for "a few lines" in a crash repair; it proposes about 20 lines in one file.
  • 8 and 9: row 604's test shape; and whether the adjudicator may choose among the library's devices for assert, deny and the bare throw, or must list them for you.
  • 10 and 11: whether you see the gate summary before the landing; free disk, 10 GB today.

Priced on batch 10 as run: about 211 agents, 36.8M (28M to 53M), of it Fable 32.9M, 89%. About 36 h in five workflows (30 to 46 h), past the process stop two or three times Pricing §3.6. No estimate of its own; none was asked.

The point both raise: rule 1 for repairs only the checker sees

  • The problem. Most of G's 57 sites and N's 60, and the drop's 18, are type slips walk does not observe. Until the switch-over, no corpus test runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library. Rule 1 asks that every edit start "from a failing test that is added to the test corpus". For these repairs no such test exists Ultra Opus §4 Blind brief.
  • Both put it first among their decisions Ultra Opus §4 Ultra Fable §4.
  • Both propose the same default. The failing evidence is the site's row in the last landed per-site list, cited. The corpus test is a guard that calls each repaired declaration with today's value, passing before and after. A site walk can see gets a failing walk test first.
  • Their strict readings differ. Ultracode Opus: a new kind of gated test that runs the checker over one library component, with G and N waiting for it. Ultracode Fable: a site without a failing test is left with a ledger row.
  • The blind pair asked it too (section 10). All four designers who worked from the content brief asked it.
  • The record answers it. A rung whose test is the checker-count or distance stage takes the last landed gate's tables as its before POSITIONS. The skill says the landed tables are a stage's before Skill. Neither rule 1 as the brief words it nor the skill says that this meets rule 1. A sentence in rule 1's text would settle it for later designers.

What the pair buys, and what the pricing cannot show

  • Ultracode Opus buys the most checks batch 10 lacked Pricing §4:
    • the brief checked against the base before work starts, 0.57M;
    • plans attacked and judged before any edit, 7.9M;
    • every piece probed by independent lenses, G and N included, 2.7M a round;
    • each finding tried by three refuters, 0.27M each;
    • test first and rule 3 enforced from the registry;
    • the distance reconciled site by site, 0.21M;
    • a final judge walking "what done means", 0.36M. That is the check that would have caught W's stop missing from your list.
    It costs about five times batch 10's tokens and five times its time.
  • Ultracode Fable buys two independent diagnoses of every group, and panels for the hardest, before any test is written (15.5M). Every review round adds a completeness critic and an independent recount of the site mapping. 33M of it is Fable Pricing §4.
  • Neither runs the check batch 10 skipped. Their gates compile the eighteen microGPT components and never run them Pricing §4.
  • Both handle recovery themselves, beyond the harness's resume from the journal: agents that continue where they stopped, branches pushed at every commit, and timed check-ins around the 13-hour stop Ultra Opus §3.3 Ultra Fable §3.
  • The pricing cannot show what either would have found that batch 10 missed. Only a run shows that; you said a real experiment compares what each run found, not only its cost Held.

    Priced: 13.7M, about 10.5 h, taking two rounds for W and G and three for C and N Pricing §3.6

  4. Integrate, record, landabout 7 agents
    • Fable Merger. Sonnet gate on a clean build, after an 8 s walk run that loads the whole library under W's new checks. On red, a Fable triage and fix, at most three times. A Fable distance reader.
    • Fable Records agent, alone; a Sonnet verifier and lander. main moves by fast-forward only.

    Priced: 1.2M, about 2.4 h Pricing §3.6

Restarts. Five workflows, each resumed with the same script and arguments, byte for byte; no clock or random value in a script. Every agent starts by recovering from its worktree's git log, its progress file and its logs' exit lines, and continues. A live background run is waited for, not restarted. Every commit is pushed at once. An empty return is retried once; a second marks the group blocked and the step goes on. Check-ins every 45 minutes and one after the predicted stop; the coordinator never presses stop. After a new session it rebuilds the next workflow's arguments from the pushed branches and the journal Ultra Fable §3.

What it puts to you Ultra Fable §4:

  • 1: rule 1 for library sites no walk test can see fail (below). Its first question.
  • 2: a testSystem run on G's and N's final code, two 4-minute runs, so a regression is traced to its piece before the merge.
  • 3: the record's folder and form, and whether main keeps the four merges or a straight history.
  • 4: the base build holds one untracked file, BASE_COMMIT, which the seeding script refuses.
  • 5 and 6: the slot count, project agent types for the preamble, and timing one reader and one group fix before the run.
  • 7: a number for "a few lines" in a crash repair; it proposes about 20 lines in one file.
  • 8 and 9: row 604's test shape; and whether the adjudicator may choose among the library's devices for assert, deny and the bare throw, or must list them for you.
  • 10 and 11: whether you see the gate summary before the landing; free disk, 10 GB today.

Priced on batch 10 as run: about 211 agents, 36.8M (28M to 53M), of it Fable 32.9M, 89%. About 36 h in five workflows (30 to 46 h), past the process stop two or three times Pricing §3.6. No estimate of its own; none was asked.

The point both raise: rule 1 for repairs only the checker sees

  • The problem. Most of G's 57 sites and N's 60, and the drop's 18, are type slips walk does not observe. Until the switch-over, no corpus test runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library. Rule 1 asks that every edit start "from a failing test that is added to the test corpus". For these repairs no such test exists Ultra Opus §4 Blind brief.
  • Both put it first among their decisions Ultra Opus §4 Ultra Fable §4.
  • Both propose the same default. The failing evidence is the site's row in the last landed per-site list, cited. The corpus test is a guard that calls each repaired declaration with today's value, passing before and after. A site walk can see gets a failing walk test first.
  • Their strict readings differ. Ultracode Opus: a new kind of gated test that runs the checker over one library component, with G and N waiting for it. Ultracode Fable: a site without a failing test is left with a ledger row.
  • The blind pair asked it too (section 10). All four designers who worked from the content brief asked it.
  • The record answers it. A rung whose test is the checker-count or distance stage takes the last landed gate's tables as its before POSITIONS. The skill says the landed tables are a stage's before Skill. Neither rule 1 as the brief words it nor the skill says that this meets rule 1. A sentence in rule 1's text would settle it for later designers.

What the pair buys, and what the pricing cannot show

  • Ultracode Opus buys the most checks batch 10 lacked Pricing §4:
    • the brief checked against the base before work starts, 0.57M;
    • plans attacked and judged before any edit, 7.9M;
    • every piece probed by independent lenses, G and N included, 2.7M a round;
    • each finding tried by three refuters, 0.27M each;
    • test first and rule 3 enforced from the registry;
    • the distance reconciled site by site, 0.21M;
    • a final judge walking "what done means", 0.36M. That is the check that would have caught W's stop missing from your list.
    It costs about five times batch 10's tokens and five times its time.
  • Ultracode Fable buys two independent diagnoses of every group, and panels for the hardest, before any test is written (15.5M). Every review round adds a completeness critic and an independent recount of the site mapping. 33M of it is Fable Pricing §4.
  • Neither runs the check batch 10 skipped. Their gates compile the eighteen microGPT components and never run them Pricing §4.
  • Both handle recovery themselves, beyond the harness's resume from the journal: agents that continue where they stopped, branches pushed at every commit, and timed check-ins around the 13-hour stop Ultra Opus §3.3 Ultra Fable §3.
  • The pricing cannot show what either would have found that batch 10 missed. Only a run shows that; you said a real experiment compares what each run found, not only its cost Held.
